title: Coin Change Problem
description: Greedy coin selection: minimizing the number of coins for change -- and exactly why it works for real currencies but breaks on arbitrary denominations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Given coin denominations and a target amount (unlimited coins of each), find the **minimum number of coins** to make that exact amount.

Rather than trying every combination (exponential time), the greedy strategy repeatedly takes the **largest denomination that still fits** -- exactly how people naturally make change: to hit 36 cents, a quarter, then a dime, then a penny.

Every cashier system, vending machine, and ATM runs some version of this algorithm behind the scenes.

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Returning 36 pennies technically works, but it's inconvenient for everyone -- systems need to minimize the coin/bill count.

**Vending machines** need fast, exact change from limited coin supplies. **ATMs** dispense optimal bill denominations to reduce mechanical wear. **Banking software** computes optimal cash distributions for bulk orders.

The same reasoning shows up in inventory packing, disk-block allocation, and schedule filling -- anywhere you're minimizing the count of "units" used to hit a target.

sections.title: Core Idea of the Greedy Strategy
sections.content:
One rule: **always take the largest coin that still fits.**

1. Sort denominations descending.
2. Start from the target amount.
3. For each denomination, while the remaining amount ≥ that coin's value, take it and subtract.

No reconsidering -- once a coin is taken, it's final.

US coins `[25, 10, 5, 1]`, target 36: take 25 (11 left), take 10 (1 left), take 1 (0 left) → **3 coins**.

sections.title: Understanding Greedy Coin Selection
sections.content:
**Philippine coins**, target 18 with `[10, 5, 1]`: 10 (8 left), 5 (3 left), three 1s → **5 coins**, optimal.

**US coins**, target 41 with `[25, 10, 5, 1]`: 25, 10, 5, 1 → **4 coins**, optimal.

**Large target**, 99 cents: three quarters (75¢) + two dimes (20¢) + four pennies → **9 coins**.

**Why order matters:** process ascending instead, and you'd take pennies repeatedly -- 99 coins instead of 9. Sorting largest-to-smallest is what makes greedy work here.

sections.title: Why the Greedy Strategy Works Here
sections.content:
Big denominations shrink the remaining amount fast, which minimizes total coin count -- but only on a **canonical coin system**, where greedy is *guaranteed* optimal for every target amount.

**Canonical examples:** US `(1,5,10,25)`, Euro `(1,2,5,10,20,50)`, Philippine pesos `(1,5,10)`.

Roughly: each coin is at least as large as the sum of all smaller ones. For US coins, a dime (10) ≥ two nickels (10) -- so a dime is never worse. Real currencies are **deliberately designed** this way so cashiers and machines can rely on simple, fast greedy logic instead of DP.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Visualization
sections.content:
Making 36 cents with `[25, 10, 5, 1]`: take a quarter (11 left) → take a dime (1 left) → take a penny (0 left). **Result: `[25, 10, 1]`, 3 coins.**

**Non-canonical** `[4, 3, 1]`, target 6: greedy takes 4 (2 left), then two 1s → `[4,1,1]`, 3 coins. **Optimal is `[3,3]`, 2 coins.** Greedy's early 4 blocked the better pairing -- proof that local choices can miss the global optimum, and that greedy only works reliably on canonical systems.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: **Basic:** sort descending, `while` loop takes coins until the remainder drops below that denomination. **Count-only:** same logic, but tracks a count instead of a list -- less memory. **Optimized (division):** skips the inner while loop entirely -- `num_coins = remaining // coin` computes the count directly, much faster on large amounts.

codeSnippets.title: Greedy Coin Change (Basic)
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 36
selected = []

# Ensure coins are sorted largest to smallest
coins.sort(reverse=True)

for coin in coins:
    while amount >= coin:
        selected.append(coin)
        amount -= coin

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Optimized Coin Change (Using Division)
codeSnippets.code:
coins = [25, 10, 5, 1]
amount = 99
coin_counts = {}

coins.sort(reverse=True)

for coin in coins:
    if amount >= coin:
        # Calculate exactly how many of this coin we need immediately
        num_coins = amount // coin
        coin_counts[coin] = num_coins
        amount -= (num_coins * coin)

print(coin_counts)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Let `n` = number of coin types, `A` = target amount.

**Basic while-loop version:** O(n) to walk denominations, but the inner while loop can run up to O(A) times (e.g. making 1 million cents in 1-cent coins) -- worst case **O(n + A)**.

**Optimized division version:** the `//` computation removes that inner loop entirely -- **O(n log n)** to sort, **O(n)** to process, independent of the amount.

**Space:** **O(1)** for just counting; **O(A / min_coin)** if you store the actual list of coins used.

chart.description: Committing immediately to large denominations, rather than exploring every combination, keeps this scalable.

sections.title: When Greedy Coin Change Fails
sections.content:
**`[1, 3, 4]`, target 6:** greedy → `[4,1,1]`, 3 coins. Optimal → `[3,3]`, 2 coins.

**`[1, 6, 10]`, target 12:** greedy → `10+1+1`, 3 coins. Optimal → `6+6`, 2 coins.

In non-canonical systems, a bigger coin isn't always better -- greedy can't see that, since it never looks ahead or backtracks. When it fails, **Dynamic Programming** guarantees the optimal answer for any coin system, at the cost of O(n × amount) time and O(amount) space.

sections.title: Why Some Currency Systems Work Well
sections.content:
**Canonical coin systems** are deliberately designed so greedy always gives the optimal answer: US `[1,5,10,25]`, Euro `[1,2,5,10,20,50]`, Philippine pesos `[1,5,10]`, Japanese yen `[1,5,10,50,100,500]`.

A sufficient condition: each coin ≥ the sum of all smaller coins (US: 5≥1, 10≥6, 25≥16). Building a cashier system for a real currency? The fast O(n) greedy algorithm is safe. Working with arbitrary or custom denominations? You need Dynamic Programming.

sections.title: Greedy vs Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
Greedy: **canonical systems only**, O(n) time (with division optimization), O(1) space.

DP: **any coin system**, O(n × amount) time, O(amount) space -- builds a table where `dp[i]` is the minimum coins for amount `i`.

Standard cashier apps: greedy, fast and correct. Puzzles or custom currencies: DP, for the correctness guarantee.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
**POS terminals** calculate minimal change and display the coin breakdown to the cashier. **Vending machines** return exact change from limited hardware tubes in real time. **ATMs** dispense optimal bill combinations to minimize stack thickness. **Banking software** determines coin/bill distributions for armored-truck cash orders.

Similar reasoning shows up in bin-packing (inventory) and blockchain UTXO selection (choosing the largest transaction inputs to minimize byte size).

subsections.title: Mistake: Assuming greedy always produces optimal solutions
subsections.content: `[1,3,4]` target 6 is the classic counterexample. Verify canonicity before trusting greedy.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring coin ordering
subsections.content: Greedy depends entirely on **descending order**. Process ascending and you'll take far too many small coins. Always sort `reverse=True`.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing greedy optimization with exhaustive search
subsections.content: Greedy commits immediately, with no lookahead -- fast, but that's also exactly why it can miss the optimal answer on tricky inputs.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The goal: **minimize the number of coins** used.
Greedy repeatedly takes the **largest denomination that fits**.
Local optimal choices **don't always** produce the global optimum.
US/Euro-style currencies are **designed for greedy correctness**.
**Dynamic Programming** is needed when greedy fails on arbitrary coins.
